old: Two lines in the same plane either intersect in exactly one point or never meet.
replacement: Two distinct lines in the same plane either intersect in exactly one point or never meet.

old: through any two points there is exactly one line.
replacement: Through any two distinct points there is exactly one line.

old: division (do the same to both sides)
replacement: division by the same nonzero number

old: It works because the radius fits around a circle exactly six times.
replacement: The radius used as a chord subtends a 60-degree central angle, so six such chords close a regular hexagon. The circumference is 2π radii, not six. At this point label the 60-degree explanation a preview, proved after Unit 5.

old: The Koch snowflake has the same 3 lines and 120 degree rotational symmetry as the equilateral triangle it grows from.
replacement: The initial equilateral triangle has 3 reflection axes and smallest positive rotation 120 degrees. The standard Koch snowflake from stage 1 onward, and in the limit, has 6 reflection axes and smallest positive rotation 60 degrees.
anchor: 8.4 pp. 319 to 324; Koch extension is original.

old: so angle APM = angle BPM.
replacement: First define M=PQ∩AB, with P and Q chosen on opposite sides of AB, and establish M lies between A and B. Then angle APQ=BPQ by SSS; because PM is ray PQ, angle APM=BPM. Continue with SAS as in UNIT04-FILL.md 4.13.

old: Ladder against a wall: why one length and a right angle suffice.
replacement: Ladder against a wall: why its length, one leg length and the right angle fix the triangle.

old: Nonvertical lines are parallel if and only if their slopes are equal.
replacement: Two distinct nonvertical lines are parallel if and only if their slopes are equal. Also, two distinct vertical lines are parallel; a vertical and a horizontal line are perpendicular.

old: An isosceles trapezoid has a pair of parallel sides (bases) and equal non-parallel sides (legs).
replacement: Under this course's inclusive trapezoid convention, define an isosceles trapezoid relative to a chosen base pair by congruent base angles, equivalently reflection symmetry exchanging the base endpoints. Rectangles count; oblique parallelograms do not. Alternatively revert everywhere to Jacobs' exclusive trapezoid convention and retain the equal-leg definition.

old: AB/WX = BC/XY = CD/YZ = DA/ZW = k
replacement: For a map ABCD to WXYZ with image/preimage scale factor k, use WX/AB=XY/BC=YZ/CD=ZW/DA=k. If using reciprocal ratios, label their common value 1/k.

old: The sides are proportional, giving A'B' = k AB with A'B' parallel to AB.
replacement: Explicitly postulate dilation preservation/scaling and line-image properties at this point, or defer their proof until after side-splitter and AA. Do not present proportional sides alone as an already-established similarity argument. Include the collinear O,A,B case separately.

old: Segment area = sector area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.
replacement: For a minor segment with central angle 0≤θ≤180 degrees, area=(θ/360)πr² minus its triangle area. A major segment has area πr² minus the complementary minor-segment area, equivalently major-sector area plus the small triangle area.

old: Slicing a cylinder parallel to its base gives a circle; tilting the plane gives an ellipse.
replacement: A plane perpendicular to a right circular cylinder's axis gives a disk. An oblique, nonaxial plane gives a full elliptical disk only when the intersection is not clipped by either finite end. A plane parallel to the axis through the interior gives a rectangle; tangent/supporting positions can be degenerate.

old: Cone, πr 2 + πrℓ.
replacement: For a right circular cone, total surface area is πr²+πrℓ. For a right circular cylinder use 2πr²+2πrh. Do not apply these simple lateral formulas to arbitrary oblique solids.

old: A regular polyhedron has congruent regular polygon faces with the same number meeting at each vertex. There are exactly five
replacement: A convex regular polyhedron has congruent regular polygon faces with the same number meeting at each vertex. There are exactly five convex regular polyhedra

old: They give the shortest path between two points along the surface.
replacement: For two distinct nonantipodal points on a sphere, the shorter great-circle arc is the unique shortest surface path. Antipodal points have infinitely many shortest semicircles. A whole great circle is not itself a shortest path.

old: On a sphere every triangle's angles add to more than 180 degrees
replacement: For a nondegenerate convex spherical triangle bounded by shorter great-circle arcs, the angle sum exceeds 180 degrees. A sphere model also differs from Euclidean incidence: antipodal points lie on infinitely many great circles.

old: Math.abs(arc - 180) < 1.5
replacement: Use a scale-relative numerical equality test for an exact diameter, or say “nearly a diameter, so nearly 90 degrees.” The display must not assert exact diameter from a 1.5-degree tolerance.

old: Math.abs(d - r) < 12
replacement: Constrain the vertex to the circle for an explicit On mode. Classify free-drag inside/outside by the true signed radius difference, except tiny scale-relative numerical tolerance. Require a separate tangent construction or limiting demonstration.

old: min: 1, max: 5, value: sk
replacement: Restrict 1≤k<n/2. If gcd(n,k)>1 describe a compound of gcd(n,k) cycles, not one n-pointed star; otherwise normalize traversal to the equivalent smaller skip.
